strengths: Well-motivated and clearly articulated problem: formalizing Instruction–Visual (IV) Complexity as the interaction of cluttered visuals and intricate instructions provides a useful lens, and the region-specific VLM–diffusion interaction insight (rather than global semantic conditioning) is a sensible and reasonably novel direction.

The training-free attention region injection mechanism (Section 3.3) is technically clean: the five attention rules (hint isolation, region/background constraints, image–latent full interaction) are clearly specified, easy to reproduce, and support parallel multi-region edits and region-level negative hints without retraining the editor.

The framework is backbone-agnostic in practice: consistent gains when applied to both Flux.1 Kontext dev and Qwen-Image-Edit (Table 1), which strengthens the claim that improvements come from planning/grounding rather than a specific editor.

A useful set of ablations is provided: planner choice (Table 2), role of CoT reasoning and staged RL (Table 3), comparison against global instruction rephrasing (Table 4), and bbox perturbation robustness (Table 5, robust up to 50% perturbation). The appendix analysis of attention-rule phenomena (Figs. 9–11) is a nice addition.

The IV-Edit benchmark (~800 manually verified pairs, 7 referring types, 16 task types) addresses a real gap: existing editing benchmarks emphasize salient objects and simple instructions. The train/test construction pipeline and category definitions are documented in the appendix.
weaknesses: The entire quantitative evaluation relies on a single LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro), while Gemini was also used to construct the benchmark instructions and to filter the data (Appendix C). This creates potential circularity and favoritism concerns, especially since a Gemini-family competitor (Gemini-Flash-Image) is evaluated by the same-family judge. No human evaluation is provided to validate the four-dimensional rubric, despite all headline claims (Overall, Weighted) resting on these judge scores.

Gains are modest and partly contradictory: on Flux Kontext, Overall improves 3.22→3.46 but Effect actually degrades (2.73→2.59), which is not clearly explained—the mechanism targets grounding/localization, but the paper should analyze why effect quality suffers. Differences of ~0.2–0.3 on a 5-point judge scale without variance/significance reporting are hard to interpret.

GRPO training details are thin: the reasoning-quality reward is simply the length of the <think> content, a crude proxy that may reward verbosity; hyperparameters, training cost, convergence behavior, and the actual composition of the 1K instruction-only samples are not given. The 'Project Page' on page 1 is blank and no code/data release is stated, hurting reproducibility.

Baseline coverage on IV-Edit is limited: strong recent region-controllable or training-free region editing approaches are absent, and closed-source models use one-shot prompting without the planning stage, which may disadvantage them. The claim of outperforming SoTA trained on 'orders of magnitude more data' is supported only by the authors' own judge-based benchmark.

Writing and polish issues suggest a rushed submission: a blank project page, typos ('VI-Edit' vs 'IV-Edit', 'anlysis', 'injectionmechanism'), inconsistent formatting in Table 4, and an appendix section titled 'Appeal of Using LLMs' containing only one sentence about LLM polishing. The conclusion overstates 'the first benchmark for IV-Complexity' given the related reasoning-editing benchmarks the paper itself cites (KrisBench, RISEBench).

Generalization scope is unclear: the attention-mask mechanism assumes an MMDiT-style joint text–image–latent architecture and would not transfer directly to UNet-based or autoregressive editors; limitations of the approach (e.g., many-region scaling, non-box-shaped regions, error cascades when the planner fails) are not discussed.

strengths: The core idea is sensible and well-motivated: refining VLM–diffusion interaction from global semantics to region-specific guidance is a plausible way to address instruction–visual complexity, and the training-free attention mask design (hint isolation, region/background constraints, full image–latent interaction) is cleanly described and supports parallel multi-region editing without iterative inpainting.

The ablation suite is more thorough than typical: planner choice (Table 2), CoT reasoning removal, staged vs. unified RL (Table 3), a global-rephrase baseline (Table 4), bbox perturbation robustness (Table 5), and qualitative attention-rule discoveries in Appendix E–F collectively probe the design choices rather than only the final system.
The paper honestly reports a trade-off: applying RePlan to Flux.1 Kontext improves Consistency (2.88→3.64) but slightly reduces Effect (2.73→2.59), which is more transparent than many editing papers.

The IV-Edit benchmark taxonomy (7 referring types × 16 task types, ~800 manually verified pairs) is a reasonable attempt to formalize a failure mode of current editing models, and the appendix provides full category definitions and data construction details.
Demonstrating the same mechanism on two MMDiT backbones (Flux Kontext Dev and Qwen-Image-Edit) provides some evidence the region-injection idea is not backbone-specific.
weaknesses: The entire evaluation rests on a single LLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) with no human study and no statistical significance testing. More critically, there is a circularity concern: Gemini-2.5-Pro is used to construct and filter the benchmark data (Appendix C), while Qwen2.5-VL-72B is used both to filter test samples and as the RL reward model. RePlan's planner is trained (GRPO) on instructions generated in exactly the same style and from the same source datasets (COCO, LISA ReasonSeg, TextSceneHQ, TableQA/TablVQA) as the test benchmark, giving it a distributional advantage over all baselines that is never disentangled from genuine capability.

The headline claim that RePlan 'consistently outperforms' SoTA is overstated. On the Weighted metric the gain over the raw Flux.1 Kontext baseline is only +0.06 (2.55 vs 2.49), and several ablation deltas (staged RL: −0.04; w/o reasoning: −0.15) are within what is plausibly judge noise given a single LLM evaluator and no variance reporting. The clearest gains are in Consistency only.

No human evaluation is provided for an image-editing paper whose central claims are perceptual (localization precision, fewer artifacts, better text editing). Given the known biases of VLM judges—especially self-family bias (Qwen2.5-VL reward model evaluating a Qwen-based planner and outputs rendered by the same attention mechanism)—human verification on at least a subset is needed to substantiate the quantitative story.

The 'reasoning quality' reward in Stage 1 is defined purely as the length of the <think> tag. This is a crude proxy that plausibly rewards verbosity rather than reasoning quality, and no analysis is given of whether longer chains actually improve plan correctness. Similarly, GRPO hyperparameters, training cost, and the number of GRPO rollouts per sample are not reported, weakening reproducibility.

The novelty claim for IV-Edit ('the first benchmark tailored to IV-Complexity') is diluted by the paper's own related-work section, which cites KrisBench and RISEBench as reasoning-oriented editing benchmarks; the differentiation rests on 'intertwined linguistic-visual complexity', which is asserted rather than empirically shown (e.g., no analysis demonstrating that methods strong on prior benchmarks specifically fail on IV-Edit).

Writing and presentation quality is below venue standard: inconsistent naming ('IV-Edit' vs. 'VI-Edit' in Section 5.1 heading), typos ('anlysis', 'futher', 'latentat', 'kongtext', 'Reservation of irrelevant regions' for 'Preservation'), an empty 'Project Page' link on page 1, and a placeholder-like Appendix A ('Appeal of Using LLMs: We use LLM for polishing writing'). These suggest the manuscript was not carefully proofread.

The prompt-injection mechanism's rules are presented as fixed design choices, but the paper lacks a systematic ablation over the five attention rules themselves (e.g., which rules are necessary); the ablations only cover the planner and RL schedule, leaving the executor-side design essentially unvalidated except anecdotally via Appendix E figures.

There is no limitations or societal-impact discussion, and no discussion of failure cases where region decomposition itself is inappropriate (e.g., globally entangled edits), despite the framework structurally assuming edits decompose into boxes.

strengths: The core idea is clear and well-motivated: refining VLM-diffusion interaction from global semantic guidance to region-specific (bbox, hint) guidance is a sensible and timely response to the observed gap between VLM grounding ability and editing models' execution ability.

The training-free attention region injection mechanism is elegant: five intuitive masking rules on MMDiT enable parallel multi-region editing, avoid degradation from multi-round inpainting, and support region-level negative hints. It requires no retraining of the editor, making it immediately applicable to both Flux.1 Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit backbones.

The two-stage GRPO strategy is well designed: format rewards first to stabilize decoding, then image-level rewards with a thoughtful reward-hacking mitigation (consistency reweighted by effect). Gains from only ~1K instruction-only samples are notable and data-efficient.

Evaluation is reasonably thorough for this type of work: two backbone variants, ablations on the planner (zero-shot vs RL), on CoT reasoning, on the staged RL strategy, a comparison against global instruction rephrasing (Appendix D), bbox overlap cases (Appendix F), and bbox perturbation robustness (Appendix G). The perturbation result (stable up to 50%) meaningfully supports practical robustness of the injection mechanism.

The IV-Edit benchmark addresses a real gap: existing editing benchmarks under-represent cluttered scenes, fine-grained referring, and reasoning-intensive edits. The taxonomy of referring types and task types is articulated in detail, and manual test-set filtering is described.

Qualitative results (Figures 6, 14-16) support the claims of better target localization and reduced editing spillover, and the framework's explicit region plans add interpretability and user controllability.
weaknesses: Potential circularity/bias in benchmark construction and evaluation: IV-Edit instructions are generated and filtered largely by Gemini 2.5 Pro / Qwen2.5-VL-72B, and the final evaluation is also performed by Gemini-2.5-Pro as a single LLM judge. No human evaluation is reported, and no agreement statistics or validation of the LLM judge against human raters are provided. Since the paper's central quantitative claims rest entirely on this protocol, this is the most significant evidentiary concern.

Gains over the underlying backbones are concentrated in Consistency (e.g., Flux: 2.88 -> 3.64) while Effect actually drops (2.73 -> 2.59 for Flux+RePlan), suggesting the mechanism trades edit-following for locality. The paper does not analyze or discuss this trade-off, nor failure modes where region injection over-constrains the edit.

RePlan does not outperform closed-source models (Gemini-Flash-Image and GPT-4o remain clearly ahead on Overall and Weighted); the claim of outperforming 'strong baselines' holds only within open-source models and mostly by modest margins (~0.2-0.4), which the framing somewhat oversells.

Using Qwen2.5-VL-72B as the reward model for Stage-2 GRPO introduces potential evaluation-model/planner-family bias, and the reliability of the Target/Effect/Consistency reward signals is not validated (e.g., correlation with human judgments of edited outputs).

Writing quality needs attention: several typos and inconsistencies ('anlysis', 'futher', 'Specificly', 'Reservation of irrelevant regions', 'Results on VI-Edit Benchmark' vs. IV-Edit, 'not belong to any region groups'), an empty 'Project Page' placeholder, and an unusual Appendix A that only says LLMs were used for polishing writing. The paper currently has no code or data release mentioned, which limits reproducibility.

Several design choices are under-justified: the five attention rules are presented as given without a systematic per-rule ablation; the effect of hyperparameters (lambda, reward caps, number of GRPO samples per instruction) is not reported; and details of how text hints are encoded into the MMDiT sequence (length/positional handling) are sparse.

The benchmark is modest in size (~800 pairs) and the multi-region subset is small (182 examples); per-category breakdowns of RePlan vs. baselines (e.g., on Knowledge/Understanding referring vs. simpler Feature referring) are not reported, so it is unclear where the gains come from across difficulty levels.
